name: Straightening hair brush

lead: A straightening brush is a heated paddle brush that smooths hair as it passes through, combining a hairbrush with the heated plates of a flat iron. The payoff is straight, sleek, neater-looking hair that is visible straight away.

Heat reshapes hydrogen bonds in the hair so it can be held straight, the same principle as a flat iron; the bonds can re-form with moisture. The first brand-name version, DAFNI, was released in 2015 after a ceramic design was patented in 2013. No dedicated studies of these brushes have been published.

paras: People brush section by section through dry hair as a quicker, one-step alternative to a flat iron, often finishing with a smoothing product. The larger heated surface covers more hair per pass, and the style holds until the next wash or until humidity and moisture bring the natural shape back.
Overuse of heated styling tools can cause severe hair damage, and hot surfaces can burn skin or scalp. Fine, bleached or already-damaged hair is more vulnerable to heat.

angle.text: A heated brush straightens and smooths hair as you brush, giving a sleeker, neater style that shows immediately and lasts until the next wash. It works on the same heat principle as a flat iron, with a wider heated surface.

lead: A straightening hair brush is a heated paddle-style brush that straightens hair as the user brushes through it, combining a hairbrush with the heated ceramic surface of a flat iron. People use it for a quicker, smoother, sleeker result, since a wide brush passes over larger sections of hair than plates clamped around narrow strands.

According to Wikipedia, a ceramic straightening brush was patented in 2013 (published 21 November 2013, with Sharon Rabi and Yakov Guy listed), and Rabi released the first one under the DAFNI brand in 2015. It has a larger heated surface than a traditional flat iron [1].

Heat straighteners work by breaking hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex, and the bonds can re-form when hair is exposed to moisture [1]. Wikipedia warns that overuse of heat tools can cause severe hair damage [1]. No published clinical study of straightening brushes was found.

paras: The brush has bristles or teeth set on a heated ceramic surface so that hair is straightened as it is combed through, instead of clamping sections between plates [1].

Heated hair tools date back to the 1870s, when French hairdresser Marcel Grateau introduced heated metal tools, and Madam C.J. Walker popularised hot combs; Isaac K. Shero patented a straightener of two heated flat irons pressed together in 1909 [1]. The ceramic straightening brush followed with the 2013 patent and the 2015 DAFNI release [1].

Straighteners break the hydrogen bonds in the hair's cortex, and those bonds re-form when the hair is exposed to moisture, which is why straightened hair can revert in humidity [1]. The plates of most modern irons are ceramic [1].

No studies specific to straightening brushes were found. Wikipedia's general warning for heated hair tools is that overuse can cause severe hair damage, although it notes that heated metal tools were gentler than early chemical straighteners [1].
No studies found. Heat straightening with flat irons has been examined in laboratory work, but no human trial of a straightening brush was identified.

timeline.event: Marcel Grateau introduces heated metal tools for hair [1].
